Ray: Good morning, nerds! It's Monday, November ninth, twenty twenty-six, and this is Nerd News Radio.

Ray: Today we start with a magnet model that refuses to order, even when you nudge it. Plus rare earths, printed jet engines, and a gravity experiment on a tiny scale.

Ada: Lots of magnetism today. I'm in.

Lead story

Ray: Okay, the lead. It's about the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model. Picture a flat grid of tiny arrows, spins, that can point anywhere in three-dimensional space. Neighbors want to line up.

Ray: A physicist named Polyakov predicted that on a flat grid, at every temperature, the correlations between distant spins die off exponentially. Nobody gets long-range order. The abstract says a proof of that was recently posted.

Ada: So that's the baseline. What's new here?

Ray: This paper asks whether that behavior is fragile. What if you make the couplings slightly unequal along the three spin directions? They show the so-called massive phase survives. For any inverse temperature, which is just temperature flipped upside down, there's a small tolerance. If the couplings stay within it of one, correlations still decay exponentially.

Ada: And what does exponential decay mean in plain words?

Ray: Two spins far apart basically forget each other, fast. The correlation length stays finite.

Ray: Then there's the easy-plane version, where spins prefer to lie in a plane. A parameter called lambda controls how much the up-down direction is penalized. Earlier work proved a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless phase, a special kind of ordering, for every lambda between minus one and one. This paper shows that its onset temperature goes to zero as lambda approaches one, the fully isotropic case.

Ada: Okay, referee hat. Is this an experiment or a simulation?

Ray: Neither. It's a mathematical proof. No measurements.

Ada: Then how good is the bound? Is small anisotropy actually small?

Ray: Here's the interesting part. The proof gives exponential decay up to a temperature scale that grows like the square root of the log of one over one minus lambda. The authors say the physical prediction is of order the log itself. So the proof is weaker than what physicists expect.

Ada: And real materials? Is the tolerance big enough to matter?

Ray: The summary doesn't say. It also says the result extends to single-ion anisotropy and to nearly isotropic models with three or more spin components.

Ada: What's the trick?

Ray: They keep the sign-cluster argument from the isotropic proof, use a known correlation inequality, and use rotation symmetry only on one finite ring, where the anisotropy is a bounded nudge. Why it matters: it shows this disordered phase is robust, not a knife-edge accident of perfect symmetry.

Magnets and materials

Ray: Staying with magnetism. A new paper tackles the two-dimensional spin one-half antiferromagnet, where Néel order, the up-down checkerboard pattern, has overwhelming evidence but no rigorous proof.

Ada: Wait, really? Nobody had proved it?

Ray: Right. This one uses a bootstrap approach, generalized inequalities, and certified energy bounds from matrix product states. It gets a strictly positive lower bound on the order parameter, including the isotropic Heisenberg point.

Ada: What's the catch?

Ray: It holds for a discrete set of anisotropy values between zero and two, not a continuum.

Ray: Next, machine learning. A supervised Transformer, the same architecture family behind chatbots, was trained on directed percolation, a model of transitions into an absorbing, dead state. It separates active from absorbing phases with high accuracy, and the critical point and exponents it yields line up closely with literature values.

Ada: Supervised means labeled data. So how much is the model just handing back what the labels told it?

Ray: The abstract doesn't answer that directly. It does show the attention patterns reorganize near criticality, and that transfer between two kinds of starting conditions works, but unevenly.

Ray: Last one. A method called DEFEAT lets a foundation model take continuous element weights, so you can optimize a crystal's composition by gradient. Of forty-five novel superconductor designs checked with density functional theory, thirty-nine passed ten kelvin, and the best reached twenty-four kelvin.

Ada: Predicted, not made.

Ray: Exactly. Calculations only.

Metal printing

Ray: Metal printing is mostly defense and industry news today. Velo3D and Sandia National Laboratories signed a five-year research agreement, a CRADA, back in January.

Ada: What's it cover?

Ray: The text doesn't say. Whether it includes monitoring or qualification is unconfirmed.

Ray: Kratos bought a large-format metal printer, the AMCM M 8K, for hypersonic manufacturing. Again, only the headline is available.

Ray: And Beehive Industries ran the first engine test of its Frenzy 6, a one hundred pound-force turbojet for small munitions and drones. Four months from finalized Air Force requirements to test.

Ada: Four months is quick. But that's the company's claim.

Ray: Yes, it is.

Weird physics corner

Ray: Now the weird stuff. Gravity is the weakest force, and almost nobody has probed it between tiny masses. This experiment, at millikelvin temperatures, has a displaced eighty-seven milligram source mass imprint its pull on a membrane carrying a one point three milligram test mass. Vibrations are read out with microwaves.

Ada: A gravitational tug between things you could barely see. Honestly, I love that.

Ray: It's a step toward testing gravity with non-classical masses, where quantum mechanics and gravity might meet. The abstract excerpt cuts off before the headline sensitivity number, though.

Ray: And in computer science, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture has been proved. If a quantum algorithm's output behaves like a low-degree polynomial in its input bits, some input bit must matter noticeably.

Ada: Which means a classical algorithm can mimic it?

Ray: On most inputs, with polynomially many queries. So big quantum speedups in the query model need extra structure, like a promise about the inputs. The abstract calls the proof elementary.

Ada: Elementary, says the mathematician, after decades. Sure.

Heisenberg model's massive phase proved stable under small anisotropy

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 7/10

The abstract reports that the two-dimensional classical Heisenberg model keeps its exponentially decaying correlations when a small anisotropy is added. For easy-plane couplings, it says the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition temperature is pushed to zero as the anisotropy parameter λ approaches 1. This clarifies how small anisotropies change ordering in 2D spin systems, though the summary does not say how useful the 'small' bound is for realistic materials.

Bootstrap proof of Néel order in 2D Heisenberg antiferromagnet

arXiv · statistical mechanics · 8/10

The abstract reports a rigorous lower bound on the Néel order parameter for the 2D S=1/2 XXZ model, including the isotropic point. The proof combines generalized Kennedy–Lieb–Shastry inequalities with certified matrix-product-state energy bounds. It settles a long-standing case where the evidence was overwhelming but no proof existed, though the bound holds only for a discrete set of Δ values rather than a continuum.

Transformer extracts critical exponents from directed percolation configurations

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports a supervised Transformer that separates active and absorbing phases, with the critical point and exponents close to literature values. Its attention patterns reorganize near criticality and show finite-size dependence. Because the model is supervised, it depends on labeled training examples, which is a natural question about how much the exponents rely on that data near the transition.

China's rare-earth export-control pause reportedly lapses with no extension published

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 7/10

Tech Times reports the pause is ending with no extension published. Only the headline is available, so the details are unconfirmed. If controls resume, it would strengthen the case for magnet designs built around cerium, a more abundant rare earth.

Rare Earth Exchanges explains China's defense supply-chain vulnerability

News · rare earths & magnets policy · 8/10

The piece covers US defense exposure to Chinese rare earths. Only the title is available, so the content is unconfirmed. Read alongside the Pentagon stockpile story, it offers background on why cerium-based magnets are attracting attention.

ML · Magnetic Materials

Neutron structure and Monte Carlo of vacancy effects in a Prussian blue magnet

arXiv · magnetism + ML · 6/10

The abstract reports a neutron-diffraction study of the magnetic structure of Co[Cr(CN)6]2/3·zH2O, with no magnetostriction at ordering. A simple Monte Carlo model suggests the ordering is robust to vacancy correlations, with minor effects only in the critical region. It is a useful example of Monte Carlo applied to real structural disorder, though it does not involve cerium.

Differentiable foundation model enables gradient-based inverse crystal design

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports DEFEAT, which lets an Equiformer model take continuous species weights so compositions can be optimized by gradient. It yields DFT-checked superconductor candidates (best 24.0 K) and photovoltaic absorber candidates. The targets are superconductivity and band gap rather than magnetism, though the idea could plausibly transfer to magnetic properties if a model for them supplied the gradients; that is inference, not a result in the abstract.

Jackknife-conformal uncertainty for ACE potentials, tested on silicon

arXiv · ML materials discovery · 5/10

The abstract reports calibrated per-atom force uncertainties for ACE potentials, propagated to 21 silicon properties and compared with Bayesian and POPS baselines. It notes failures for relaxed point defects and under-coverage for left-out screw dislocations. It matters for uncertainty quantification when data are scarce, though the demonstration is on silicon rather than magnets. The related physics-informed POPS prior paper covers a similar theme.

Valence transition and phase coexistence in substituted EuPd2Si2

Physical Review Materials · 5/10

A PRMaterials paper on the tunable valence transition in EuPd2Si2, which responds to temperature, pressure and field. It is f-electron valence physics, a close cousin of rare-earth magnetism. Only a truncated abstract is available, so the findings are unconfirmed.

Additive Manufacturing

Velo3D and Sandia sign five-year metal 3D printing CRADA

TCT Magazine · 6/10

TCT reports a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement signed in January 2026, and TradingView also covers it. The scope is not in the text, so whether it includes monitoring or qualification is unconfirmed. It is worth watching for any shared data or sensor work.

eSharp: diffusion-based event-camera metric depth estimation

arXiv · event-based vision · 4/10

The abstract reports event-only monocular depth estimation using diffusion priors, trained with LiDAR-calibrated pseudo-labels from a co-registered frame camera. It is general depth sensing rather than melt-pool monitoring. The cross-modal pseudo-label idea is generally relevant to event-camera research.

Kratos buys AMCM M 8K large-format metal AM system

News · AM policy & funding · 5/10

Defense and Munitions reports Kratos acquired the system for hypersonic manufacturing. Only the headline is available. It signals defense capacity in additive manufacturing and interest in monitoring and qualification for large builds.

Beehive's 100 lbf Frenzy 6 turbojet completes first engine test

3D Printing Industry · 5/10

3D Printing Industry reports the engine went from finalized Air Force requirements to a first test in four months. It is a sign of defense adoption of additive manufacturing rather than monitoring research. The speed claim comes from the company.

Theoretical Physics

Exact solution of ±J Edwards-Anderson model in a transverse field

arXiv · spin models & criticality · 7/10

The abstract reports that in a Majorana representation, a Z2 gauge freedom removes the sign disorder, so the spectrum matches the uniform model. The spin-glass order parameter vanishes above a critical transverse field and equals 1/4 below it. The result sits close to the transverse-field Ising and LiHoF4 literature; how the quadratic Majorana treatment relates to the full interactions of the real model is a question the summary leaves open.

Symmetry-based finite-size scaling finds dissipative critical points

arXiv · quantum physics · 7/10

The abstract reports a framework for the 2D dissipative XYZ model in which sensitivity to a weak symmetry shows finite-size scaling and yields a critical-point estimate. It applies to open quantum systems rather than closed ones. The paper also proposes a circuit algorithm built on mid-circuit measurements.

Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture proved: low-degree polynomials have influential variables

arXiv · quantum physics · 7/10

Plainly: if a quantum algorithm's output behaves like a low-degree polynomial of its input bits, some input bit must matter noticeably. The abstract says this implies a classical algorithm with polynomially many queries can approximate the quantum one on most inputs. So superpolynomial quantum speedups in the query model need extra structure, such as a promise on the inputs. The abstract calls the proof elementary.

Millikelvin experiment measures gravity from an 87 mg source mass

arXiv · gravity & cosmology · 6/10

Gravity is so weak that it has barely been probed between tiny masses. The abstract reports a membrane with a 1.3 mg test mass sensing the pull of a coherently displaced 87 mg source in a microwave optomechanical setup. It is a step toward testing gravity with non-classical masses, where quantum mechanics and gravity may meet.
